Designing tools an agent can use

fieldEntries.title: Keeping a research coding framework, losing the tagging
fieldEntries.summary: Qualitative researchers were spending their time applying a coding framework to transcripts by hand. The framework stayed theirs; the repetitive application did not.

quote.text: Our researchers stopped tagging transcripts and started interpreting them. The coding framework is still ours — the machine just keeps up with it now.
quote.name: Name Surname

body.text: A qualitative coding framework is a research instrument. It is developed deliberately, it evolves slowly, and its consistency is what makes findings comparable across a study. Any system that quietly reinterprets it is worse than no system.
The constraint that shaped everything

The framework had to remain the researchers'. That ruled out an approach where the model invents its own categories from the data, and it made the codebook the specification rather than the training data — the categories, their definitions, and their boundary cases are the prompt.
How drift was kept visible

items: **Every applied code carries the passage it came from**, so a researcher can check the application rather than trust it.
**A held-out set of researcher-coded transcripts** is the evaluation set. Agreement with the humans is the metric, per code, not overall.
**Codebook changes re-run the set.** A refined definition that improves one code and degrades two is visible before it is adopted.
**Disagreements are surfaced, not resolved.** Where the model and the codebook are in tension, that is a finding about the codebook.

body.title: What this deliberately does not do
body.text: It does not discover themes, and it does not merge codes it judges similar. Both are research decisions, and a system that made them would be making claims the researchers had not.

fieldEntries.title: Discovery: finding out where AI pays back
fieldEntries.summary: A structured audit of a workflow, the data behind it, and what a win would measurably look like — before anything is built and before anyone commits to a scope.

facts.v: A scope, a timeline, an estimate

body.text: Discovery exists to answer one question honestly: is there a workflow here where a model earns its cost, and what would have to be true for that to hold? A discovery that concludes "not yet" is a successful discovery.
What gets audited

head: Area
What we are looking for
rows: Who does it, how often, what the variation actually is
Whether it exists, whether it is reachable, and who may see it
What is deterministic and undocumented versus genuinely judgement-based
What happens when the system is wrong, and who notices
What a win looks like as a number that already exists

body.text: The last row is the one that most often ends a project early, and it should. If nobody can say what improvement would look like in a number the business already tracks, there is nothing to evaluate against later.
What comes out
A fixed scope, a timeline and an estimate built from the requirement rather than from a rate card — and, where the answer is that the workflow is not ready, what would have to change first.

learn.label: Choosing a model for the workload

fieldEntries.title: Build and evaluate: weekly increments, gates before production
fieldEntries.summary: Delivery in weekly increments with evaluation gates, so quality is a measurement rather than an opinion by the time anything touches production.

body.text: The failure mode of an AI build is not that it does not work — it is that nobody can say whether it works better than last week. Evaluation is therefore the first deliverable rather than the last.

items: **Week one produces an evaluation set**, drawn from real inputs, before there is anything to evaluate.
**Each increment reports against it**, per tag rather than as one average.
**A gate before production**: no case regresses, and the production signal that matters has been agreed.
**Rollout is staged** behind a flag, compared live, and reversible by configuration.
**Handover is the plan**, not an afterthought: your code, your documentation, your team trained on it.

body.title: Why the evaluation set comes first
body.text: It is the artefact that outlives the engagement. Long after the delivery team has gone, it is what tells the client whether a prompt change, a model upgrade or a new corpus made things better.
Managed operation afterwards is available and optional. The default assumption is that the client owns and runs what was built.

fieldEntries.title: Agent migration: moving workflows off a platform
fieldEntries.summary: Recovering evaluation sets from production traces, translating workflows through a canonical representation, and proving equivalence before any traffic moves.

body.text: A platform migration is usually presented as a code problem and is almost always an intent problem: the workflow encodes decisions nobody wrote down, and the risk is changing them without noticing.
Sequence

items: Inventory every workflow and its dependants. A meaningful share are usually dormant and do not need migrating at all.
Recover evaluation sets from production traces — without them, equivalence is an opinion.
Translate through a canonical intermediate representation rather than rebuilding, so the migration is reviewable as a workflow.
Shadow-run against live traffic with side effects disabled.
Switch a share of traffic, compare production signals, then move the rest.

body.text: The parts that never transfer — connectors, managed memory, identity and secrets — are named at inventory time, because they are the difference between an estimate and a surprise.

body.title: The accelerator is open
body.text: The intermediate representation and pipeline are [Wheatear](/projects/wheatear), which is public. The engagement is the migration; the tool is not the deliverable.

pages.title: Introduction
pages.summary: What OpenLCM is for, and the failure it exists to remove.

body.text: OpenLCM is a memory layer for AI agents. It stores every message verbatim and compresses that history into a hierarchical structure, so an agent can recall any past moment while the context it actually sends stays inside a bounded window.
The failure it removes

Long conversations outgrow the context window. The three usual responses each lose something: a sliding window drops old turns silently, summarisation loses specifics unpredictably, and sending everything is unaffordable and eventually impossible. The visible symptom is an assistant that contradicts a decision made forty turns ago.

head: Approach
History
Context size
Recall
rows: Complete, until it will not fit

body.text: What you get

items: **Message persistence** — every message stored in SQLite with full-text search over it.
**A summary DAG** — leaf nodes compressed into session summaries and then into durable history.
**A fact store** — decisions, constraints and preferences held as addressable facts rather than left in prose.
**A code graph** — repositories parsed into a semantic tree so agents can navigate code rather than grep it.
**Framework adapters** — LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, Google ADK, and the OpenAI and Anthropic clients.
**Agent-callable tools** — recall and search exposed to the agent, not only to the host application.

body.title: When you do not need this
body.text: A single-turn task, or an assistant whose conversations are short by design, does not need a memory layer. Reach for it when history is long, when decisions made earlier must bind later behaviour, or when you need history to be auditable.

pages.title: Installation
pages.summary: Install from PyPI; the store is a SQLite file.

body.text: OpenLCM is pure Python with a SQLite backend — no compiled extensions and no separate service to run. It works on macOS, Linux and Windows.

body.code:
pip install openlcm

# or with uv
uv add openlcm

body.text: The store is a file. That is a deliberate property rather than a limitation: it can be inspected with ordinary SQLite tooling, copied, and committed to a fixture for tests.

body.title: Treat the store as production data
body.text: It contains the full text of every message. Apply the same retention, redaction and access rules you would apply to any conversation log — see Privacy and retention.
For exact version requirements and optional extras, check the repository README — this guide deliberately does not restate them, because they change.

pages.title: Quick start
pages.summary: Record a conversation, then recall from it without replaying the transcript.

body.text: The shape of every integration is the same: record messages as they happen, and ask for context when you are about to call the model. What comes back is bounded; what is stored is not.

body.code:
from openlcm import Memory

memory = Memory(path="./conversations.db", session="customer-4471")

# Record as the conversation happens — verbatim, nothing dropped.
memory.add("user", "We moved off the legacy plan last year.")
memory.add("assistant", "Noted — I'll use the current plan for pricing.")

# Ask for context at call time, with a token budget you control.
context = memory.context(query=question, budget=4_000)

reply = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL,
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=SYSTEM,
    messages=[*context.messages, {"role": "user", "content": question}],
)

body.text: The `budget` argument is the important one. It is what makes context a bounded input rather than a growing one, and it is where the compression structure earns its place — the layer decides what to include, expand or summarise to fit.

body.title: Signatures
body.text: Argument names and return shapes are illustrative. Check the repository for the current API before writing an integration against it.

pages.title: The memory model
pages.summary: Three layers — messages, summaries, facts — and which question each answers.

body.text: OpenLCM separates memory into three layers because they answer different questions. Conflating them is what makes home-grown memory systems drift.

body.caption: Complete history, bounded context
body.art:
every message        →  stored verbatim, full-text indexed
       ↓ compress
session summaries    →  one per session
       ↓ compress
durable history      →  the long arc
       ↓ select
this turn's context  →  facts + relevant summaries + recent turns

body.text: Only the bottom row is sent to the model. Everything above it is available, and any summary can be expanded back to the messages beneath it — which is what makes the compression recoverable rather than lossy.

pages.title: The summary DAG
pages.summary: Why compression is a graph rather than a running summary.

body.text: A running summary rewritten on every turn accumulates drift: each rewrite is a paraphrase of a paraphrase, and there is no way back to what was actually said. OpenLCM compresses into a directed acyclic graph instead, where every node records the nodes it compresses.

items: **Leaf nodes** cover a small span of messages.
**Session nodes** compress the leaves of one session.
**Durable nodes** compress sessions into the long arc of the relationship.

body.text: Why the edges matter

Because each node points at what it summarises, recall can start broad and descend. An agent asked about a decision can read the durable layer, identify the session, and expand to the exact messages — spending context only where it is needed rather than paying for detail up front.

body.title: Regenerable by design
body.text: Summaries are derived, so improving the summarisation prompt does not mean losing history. Messages are the source of truth; the DAG can be rebuilt.

pages.title: The fact store
pages.summary: The facts that must survive compression, held as addressable keys.

body.text: Some statements must bind future behaviour regardless of how old they are: a plan the customer is on, a constraint they stated, a correction they issued. Those do not belong in prose that a summariser is free to paraphrase away.

body.code:
memory.facts.put("billing.plan", "current", source=message_id)
memory.facts.put("comms.no_marketing", True, source=message_id)

# Included in every turn's context — small, explicit, always present.
facts = memory.facts.all(prefix="billing.")

body.text: Promotion is a policy

Not everything said deserves to be a fact. Decide deliberately what gets promoted — commitments, constraints, corrections — and leave the rest in ordinary history where it remains retrievable but does not occupy the window.

body.title: Supersede, do not append
body.text: Writing a second value for the same key must replace the first, with the source recorded. A fact store that accumulates contradictory values is worse than no fact store, because the model will see both.
Every fact carries its source message, which is what makes the store auditable: "why does it think that?" resolves to a specific turn rather than to a summary.

pages.title: The code graph
pages.summary: Parsing a repository into a semantic tree so an agent can navigate rather than grep.

body.text: A coding agent given a repository as raw text spends its context reading files to find out where things are. OpenLCM parses repositories into a Lossless Semantic Tree — a graph of definitions and their relationships — so navigation is a lookup rather than a scan.

items: Find a definition without reading the file it lives in.
Walk callers and callees rather than searching for a name.
Load only the nodes a task needs into the window.

body.text: "Lossless" is the important word: the tree carries the structure, and the original source remains addressable through it. The agent gets a map, and can still read the territory.

body.title: Language coverage
body.text: Parsing depends on the languages supported by the current release. Check the repository before assuming a language is covered.

pages.title: Using it with a framework
pages.summary: Adapters for the common agent frameworks and clients.

body.text: OpenLCM ships adapters for LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen and Google ADK, and for the OpenAI and Anthropic clients directly. The adapter's job is to record messages and inject context at the right point in that framework's lifecycle, so adopting it is not a rewrite.

body.code:
# The pattern every adapter follows: wrap, and let the framework run.
from openlcm.adapters import anthropic as lcm

client = lcm.wrap(anthropic_client, memory=memory)

# Calls now record automatically and receive bounded context.
reply = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024, messages=turns)

body.text: Without an adapter

The manual integration is two calls — `add` after each message and `context` before each request — which is worth doing directly if your orchestration is your own. Adapters exist to avoid touching framework internals, not because the API is complicated.

body.title: Record both sides
body.text: Recording user turns and not assistant turns produces a history that reads as a monologue and summarises badly. Both sides, always.

pages.title: Exposing memory as tools
pages.summary: Letting the agent search its own history instead of pre-fetching for it.

body.text: OpenLCM can expose recall, history search, semantic search and code navigation as tools the agent calls itself. That shifts the decision about what to remember from your code to the model — useful for exploratory work, and worth bounding.

head: Pre-fetch context
Memory as tools
rows: The agent digs when it needs to
The model refines its own query
Harder to bound — set a step limit

body.text: A reasonable default is both: seed the context with facts and recent turns, and expose search for the cases where the agent needs something older. That keeps the common path cheap and the rare path possible.

body.title: Tool results cost context too
body.text: A history search returning fifty messages has spent the budget the task needed. Page results and return spans rather than whole sessions.

pages.title: Evaluating recall
pages.summary: Measuring whether the memory layer actually remembers, rather than assuming it.

body.text: A memory system is a retrieval system, and it should be measured like one. The repository includes runs against long-context memory benchmarks; your own corpus deserves the same treatment, because your conversations are not the benchmark's.

items: Take real conversations and write questions whose answers appear only in early turns.
Record which message contains each answer — that is your label.
Run recall at your production context budget, not an unlimited one.
Measure how often the answering message is reachable from the returned context.
Re-run whenever the summarisation prompt, the budget, or the compression settings change.

body.text: The distinction that matters is between "the fact was in the window" and "the fact was in the store". A store that holds everything and a context that never surfaces it is a system that forgets, whatever the persistence layer says.

pages.title: Privacy and retention
pages.summary: What the store contains, and the obligations that follow.

body.text: The store holds the verbatim text of every message. That is the feature — and it means the file inherits every obligation that applies to conversation data.

items: **Redact at write time** where a category of data should never be stored, rather than filtering on read.
**Set a retention period** per session or per tenant, and enforce deletion rather than documenting it.
**Support erasure.** A request to be forgotten must remove messages, the summaries derived from them, and any facts sourced from them.
**Treat the file as privileged.** Access to the store is access to every conversation.
**Separate tenants** into separate stores where the data-protection posture requires it.

body.title: Erasure has to cascade
body.text: Deleting messages while leaving the summaries derived from them keeps the content in paraphrased form. Any deletion path must invalidate and regenerate the affected summary nodes.

pages.title: Troubleshooting
pages.summary: Symptoms, causes, and what to check first.

body.text: The agent still forgets things

Check whether the fact was ever promoted. A preference stated in passing lives in message history, and if the context budget did not surface that session it is effectively absent. Promote commitments and corrections to facts at the moment they are made.
Context is still overflowing

The budget passed to `context` is the layer's allocation, not the whole window. Reserve room for the system prompt, tool schemas and the answer — a budget equal to the window will always overflow once output is added.
Recall returns the wrong session

Usually a session-keying problem: several conversations recorded under one session id, or a new id per request so nothing accumulates. Check that the session key matches the unit you actually mean by "a conversation".
The store is growing quickly
Expected — it holds everything. Manage it with retention rather than by dropping messages: archive or delete whole sessions past their period, and regenerate the affected summary nodes.

pages.title: Introduction
pages.summary: What Wheatear is for, and who it is aimed at.

body.text: Wheatear is an accelerator for moving AI agents and workflows between orchestration platforms. It parses a source workflow into a canonical intermediate representation and generates the target from it, turning a rebuild into a reviewable, testable migration.
The problem

An agent workflow built in a vendor designer is expressed in that vendor's state model, connectors and control flow. Moving it normally means reading the design, inferring what it was meant to do, rebuilding it elsewhere, and hoping the behaviour matches. The expensive part is not the code — it is re-deriving intent that was never written down.
Who it is for

Enterprise architects, platform and integration engineers, and technical decision-makers evaluating a platform switch. The project documents itself with real IR snippets and pipeline traces rather than marketing diagrams, because that audience judges an accelerator by its artefacts.

body.title: It is an accelerator, not a button
body.text: A migration still needs review and testing. What Wheatear removes is the manual re-derivation of structure — which is most of the work and nearly all of the risk of silent behaviour change.

pages.title: How it works
pages.summary: Parse, transform, generate — with the IR as the seam.

body.caption: One parser per source, one generator per target
body.art:
source platform ──parse──▶ canonical IR ──generate──▶ target platform
                              │
                              ├── diffable: review the workflow, not the code
                              ├── testable: run the same cases against both
                              └── reusable: N + M adapters instead of N × M paths

body.text: The IR is the point. Without it, every source-to-target pair is its own migration tool; with it, adding a platform means writing one parser or one generator and inheriting every existing pairing.
Three stages

items: **Parse.** Read the source workflow — exported definition, configuration, or code — into steps, tools, transitions and conditions.
**Transform.** Normalise into the canonical IR. This stage is deterministic, because it is where correctness is decided.
**Generate.** Emit the target platform's representation from the IR, with the parts that have no equivalent flagged rather than silently dropped.

body.text: The flagging matters as much as the generation. A construct with no target equivalent is a decision for a human, and a tool that quietly omits it produces a workflow that looks complete and is not.

pages.title: The intermediate representation
pages.summary: A platform-neutral description of what a workflow does.

body.text: The IR describes a workflow in terms every platform has: steps, the tools they invoke, the transitions between them, and the conditions on those transitions. Platform-specific detail is carried as annotations rather than being baked into the structure.

body.code:
id: refund-triage
entry: classify
steps:
  - id: classify
    kind: model_call
    prompt_ref: prompts/classify.md
    output: { schema: RefundIntent }
    transitions:
      - when: "intent == 'refund'"
        to: check_eligibility
      - default: handoff

  - id: check_eligibility
    kind: tool_call
    tool: billing.get_order
    inputs: { order_id: "$.intent.order_id" }
    on_error: handoff

body.text: Because it is structured text, the IR is diffable. That is what lets a migration be reviewed as a change to a workflow rather than as a wall of generated code — and it is what makes a second migration cheap.

pages.title: Deterministic and assisted stages
pages.summary: Which parts are code, which parts use a model, and why the split falls there.

body.text: Wheatear is deliberate about where model assistance is used. Structural transformation is deterministic; assistance is applied only where the source genuinely does not state its intent.

body.text: The reason for the split is reviewability. A deterministic transformation can be trusted and spot-checked; an inferred intent must be read by a human, and it is far easier to review when it is isolated to a labelled part of the output.

body.title: Review the inferred parts
body.text: Anything the pipeline inferred is a hypothesis about what the original authors meant. It is usually right and occasionally confidently wrong — which is exactly why it is separated from the parts that are not guesses.

What transfers
The right-hand column is not a gap in the tool — it is the part of a migration that is genuinely re-implementation. Naming it early is what keeps a migration estimate honest.

pages.title: Planning a migration
pages.summary: Sequencing the work so the risky part happens last.

items: **Inventory.** List every workflow, its triggers, its tools, and who depends on it. Half of them are usually dormant.
**Recover evaluation sets.** Capture real tasks and their outcomes from production traces. Without these, "it works the same" is an opinion.
**Migrate something low-risk first.** The second migration is far cheaper than the first; pay the learning cost where it does not matter.
**Do the critical ones with the pipeline proven**, and shadow-run them before any traffic moves.
**Extract the portable assets as you go** — prompts, tool contracts and evaluation sets into your own repository.

body.title: The last step is the one that pays twice
body.text: Prompts and evaluation sets kept in your own version control are what stop the next migration from being this expensive.
Expect the inventory to shrink the project. Workflows that nobody triggers do not need migrating, and finding them is often the single largest saving in the plan.

pages.title: Proving equivalence
pages.summary: Comparing outcomes rather than transcripts, and switching traffic on evidence.

body.text: Two agents will not produce identical text, and they do not need to. What must match is behaviour: the same tools called with the same arguments, the same escalations, the same final state.

items: Run the recovered case set against both implementations with tool calls recorded.
Compare outcomes and tool traces, not wording. Different phrasing with the same action taken is a pass.
Shadow-run the target against live traffic with side effects disabled.
Switch a small share of traffic and compare production signals — escalation rate, completion rate, cost per task.
Keep the rollback a configuration change until the comparison is boring.

body.title: Disable side effects in shadow mode
body.text: A shadow run that issues real refunds is not a shadow run. Route writing tools to a recorder before pointing any traffic at the new implementation.

pages.title: Troubleshooting
pages.summary: The failures a migration actually produces.

body.text: The generated workflow is missing a branch

Check the flagged constructs in the pipeline output. A branch with no equivalent on the target is reported rather than emitted, and it is a decision for a human — silently dropping it is the failure mode this behaviour exists to prevent.
Behaviour differs only on edge cases

Usually an inferred condition. Look at the model-assisted portion of the IR: a branch whose intent had to be recovered is the most likely place for a subtle mismatch. Compare against the source definition and correct the IR rather than patching the generated output.
Tools work in isolation but fail in the migrated workflow

Almost always identity or secrets — the part that never transfers. Confirm the target is calling with the right principal, and that the tool enforces authorisation itself rather than relying on a connector the old platform provided.
The comparison run is inconclusive
The case set is too small or too easy. Recover more cases from production traces, weighted towards the ones that escalated or failed — those are the behaviours a migration is most likely to change.
